questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A repeated value under a declared key
questions.learningObjective: state what a declared key does to a second row carrying the same value
questions.stem: A customer table declares cust_id as its primary key and already holds one row with cust_id 1. An insert arrives carrying cust_id 1 again with a different name. What does the declared key do to that write?

options.text: The write is refused, because the key has to single out exactly one row
Both rows are kept, because a table may hold the same key value twice
options.misconception: believes a table can hold two rows under one declared key

options.text: The new row quietly overwrites the row that was already stored
options.misconception: believes a key collision overwrites the earlier row silently

options.text: The write goes through, because the two rows carry different names
options.misconception: believes differing non-key values make a repeated key acceptable

questions.explanation: A declared key is what makes the rows of a table a set rather than a pile: exactly one row may sit under each key value, so a second row with the same value is refused and the run returned a uniqueness failure naming the key column. Two rows under one key would make every question of the form which one and how many ambiguous, and a table that allowed them could not be pointed at by anything else. Keeping both is only possible where no key is declared, and comparing the names misses the point, because the key is the identity of a row rather than its description.
questions.hint: Ask how many rows one key value is allowed to identify.

questions.topic: What a repeating group is
questions.learningObjective: identify a repeating group in a cell and say what it costs
questions.stem: One enrolment table has columns for student, course and scores, and the scores cell holds the text "7,8,9". What makes that cell a repeating group rather than an ordinary value?

options.text: The cell holds several values in one place, so each has no column of its own
The cell holds text, so arithmetic on it would need a conversion first
options.misconception: believes the fault is only the stored type rather than several values

options.text: The cell holds digits, so it is narrower than a whole number column
options.misconception: believes the fault is the width of the stored value

options.text: The cell holds three values, so the table is wider than its three columns
options.misconception: believes a repeating group makes a table wider rather than packed

questions.explanation: A repeating group is several values of the same kind sharing one cell, and because none of them has a column of its own, no single one can be named in a filter, constrained, joined or indexed; a question about the third score has to split the text first. Three packed cells in the sample split into five separate score values, and five is the row count a design of one value per row would hold. Converting the text to numbers changes the type and not the addressing problem, and three columns is still three columns however many values the third one holds.
questions.hint: Ask how a filter would reach the third score in that cell.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The anomaly first normal form prevents
questions.learningObjective: name the anomaly that one value per cell removes
questions.stem: Replacing the packed scores cell with columns named score1, score2 and score3 puts the table into first normal form. Which anomaly does that change actually prevent?

options.text: A fourth result cannot be filed, so a course with four scores loses one
A course cannot be deleted, so its results stay in the table for good
options.misconception: confuses the change with a deletion anomaly about course rows

options.text: A student cannot be renamed, so the old name survives in every copy
options.misconception: confuses the change with an update anomaly about a student name

options.text: A course cannot be added, so a new subject has no row to sit in
options.misconception: confuses the change with an insertion anomaly about a course row

questions.explanation: First normal form is one value per cell, and its payoff is that the number of values is no longer fixed by the column list, so a fourth score needs a new row rather than a fourth column and nothing is dropped. The other three are real anomalies, but they belong to the two later forms: a course that cannot be recorded until it has an enrolment is an insertion problem, and a name that has to be edited in every copy is an update problem, and neither is cured by unpacking a cell. Choosing the answer that describes a lost value is what makes this item hard rather than the vocabulary.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a course holding more results than the columns allow.

questions.topic: The anomaly second normal form prevents
questions.learningObjective: name the anomaly that removing a partial dependency prevents
questions.stem: A flat enrolment table is keyed on the pair (student, course) and also stores student_name, course_title and credits. Which anomaly does second normal form prevent in this table?

options.text: Changing a course's credits means editing every row where that course appears
A student with no enrolments cannot be recorded in the table at all
options.misconception: believes second normal form is about recording an empty related table

options.text: Two students on one course produce two copies of the course title
options.misconception: believes second normal form removes the course row rather than the repeat

options.text: A course with no students cannot be recorded in the table at all
options.misconception: believes second normal form is about courses that have no students

questions.explanation: Second normal form removes a partial dependency, meaning a non-key column that depends on only part of a composite key, and the anomalies it prevents are the update ones. Credits depend on the course alone, so the credits of one course sit in each of the rows where it appears, and in this table that is two rows, which both have to be found and edited or the table will report two different values for one course. The other two answers describe insertion anomalies, which happen to a student or a course with no related rows and are real, but they are not what this form is about.

questions.topic: Repairing a partial dependency
questions.learningObjective: choose the change that removes a partial dependency
questions.stem: In a table keyed on (student_id, course_id), the student_name column depends on student_id alone and not on course_id. Which change removes that partial dependency?

options.text: Move student_name into a students table keyed on student_id by itself
Move student_name to sit after the key columns in the column list
options.misconception: believes column position changes what a value depends on

options.text: Add a single integer column to stand in for the composite key
options.misconception: believes renaming the key removes a dependency on part of it

options.text: Split student_name into two columns called first_name and last_name
options.misconception: believes breaking one value into two columns removes the dependency

questions.explanation: A partial dependency is repaired by putting the partly dependent column in a table whose whole key is the part it truly depends on, so a students table keyed on student_id holds the name once and the enrolment table stops repeating it. Moving a column changes nothing about which values it depends on, and a new integer key only renames what was already there, leaving the name still hanging off one part of it. Splitting a name into two columns keeps every part of the problem, because each half depends on exactly the same half of the key as before.
questions.hint: Ask what the whole key of the name's own table would be.

questions.topic: What a transitive dependency is
questions.learningObjective: recognise a chain of two non-key columns as a transitive dependency
questions.stem: A course table holds course_id, department and dept_office, and dept_office is fixed by the department while the department is fixed by the course_id. What is that arrangement?

options.text: A transitive dependency, since the office is fixed through the department
A partial dependency, since the office depends on part of the key
options.misconception: confuses a chain through two columns with a split across a composite key

options.text: A repeating group, since each course carries an office in every row
options.misconception: confuses one office column with a group of repeated values

options.text: A reference, since the office column points at another table's office
options.misconception: confuses a column derived from another with a stored pointer to a row

questions.explanation: A transitive dependency is a chain in which one non-key column determines another, so the course fixes the department and the department fixes the office, which means the office is determined by the course without the course naming it directly. That is not a partial dependency, which needs a composite key to be split across, and it is not a repeating group, because one office value sits in one cell rather than several. Calling it a reference misses the point as well: no stored value names a row in another table, the office is derived from a column beside it.
questions.hint: Ask how many hops away from the key the office value sits.

questions.topic: The anomaly third normal form prevents
questions.learningObjective: name the anomaly that removing a transitive dependency prevents
questions.stem: Every course row names a department and repeats that department's office, so moving the office means touching each course. Which anomaly does third normal form prevent?

options.text: One office has to be edited in every course row that repeats it
A course in a brand new department cannot be filed without an office
options.misconception: believes third normal form is about which values a course may carry

options.text: A department that owns no course has no row in which to keep its office
options.misconception: believes third normal form is what makes an empty related table possible

options.text: Two courses in one department can end up disagreeing about its office
options.misconception: believes third normal form is a rule about rows agreeing with each other

questions.hint: Ask how many rows would need editing to move one office.

questions.topic: The trade in a deliberate denormalisation
questions.learningObjective: state what a deliberate denormalisation buys and what it costs
questions.stem: Order lines store a copy of the product name so a sales report reads one table instead of joining. The product is then renamed. What has the team bought and what have they paid for it?

options.text: Reports that skip a join, paid for with copies that can fall behind the source
A smaller stored dataset, paid for with reports that stop being trusted
options.misconception: believes denormalising removes redundancy rather than moving it

options.text: Stronger integrity on the product table, paid for with a slower rename
options.misconception: believes denormalising improves the integrity of the source table

options.text: Fewer repeated values on disk, paid for with a lost reference check
options.misconception: believes denormalising deletes a repeated name out of the storage

The stored rows did not shrink, since the name is still written once per line, and nothing about the product table's own integrity improved.

questions.topic: Column order inside a composite index
questions.learningObjective: predict which queries one composite index can serve from its column order
questions.stem: One index is declared on the pair (cust_id, order_date) over a table that also holds an amount column. Which single query can that index serve?

options.text: Filter on cust_id and order the customer's rows by date
Filter on order_date alone, since it is the second indexed column
options.misconception: believes a later column of a composite index can be entered on its own

options.text: Filter on amount, since the index is built over the whole table
options.misconception: believes the index covers columns the table never put in it

options.text: Count every row in the table, since an index always holds them all
options.misconception: believes an index stores whole rows so any scan can be served

questions.topic: Primary key against a unique rule
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a primary key from a unique rule on another column
questions.stem: A table already declares id as its primary key, and a second rule marks the email column UNIQUE. What does the second rule add that the first does not already give?

options.text: A further set of values no two rows may share, on a chosen column
A second stored copy of the primary key, kept in step on every write
options.misconception: believes a unique rule is a duplicate storage of the key column

options.text: A guarantee that email is never blank, which the primary key lacks
options.misconception: believes uniqueness also requires a value to be present

options.text: Permission for two rows to share an id, which a unique rule forbids
options.misconception: believes a unique rule loosens what the primary key requires

questions.explanation: The primary key is the one designated column or set of columns that identifies a row and that other tables point at, and it can be declared only once. A unique rule is a promise about a column picked for lookups, and any number of them can sit side by side, which is how a table insists an address appears at most once while still allowing it to be left blank, since a run of two blanks is accepted. Together the two are the usual pairing, and neither is a stored copy of the other.

questions.topic: The default behaviour of a reference on delete
questions.learningObjective: state what happens by default when a referenced row is deleted
questions.stem: A child table's parent_id references a parent table's id, and two child rows point at parent 1. A statement deletes parent 1. What happens?

options.text: The delete is refused, because the children would point at nothing
The delete goes through, and the children keep the old value in place
options.misconception: believes a child may be left pointing at a row that is gone

options.text: The delete goes through, and the two children are removed with it
options.misconception: believes a reference silently deletes the rows that point at the parent

options.text: The delete goes through, but only where the parent had no children
options.misconception: believes the rule is applied only where nothing points at the row

options.text: In a nightly report, so the table can be corrected in bulk

questions.topic: A blank that means unknown and a blank that means not applicable
questions.learningObjective: separate a missing measurement from a value that does not apply
questions.stem: A middle_school column names a building for secondary schools and is left blank for primary schools. Why is that not one kind of blank but two?

A blank can mean a recorded zero, and zero is a different number entirely

options.text: A blank can mean an empty piece of text, which sorts differently

questions.topic: Preventing a lost update with a version column
questions.learningObjective: explain how a version column turns a lost update into a failed write
questions.stem: Two sessions read a balance of 100, both take off 10 and both write 90. A version column is added and a write must also match the version that was read. What does the second write do?

options.text: It changes no rows, because the version it read has been superseded
It overwrites the first write, because the version is read after the value
options.misconception: believes a version column recomputes a value rather than refusing a write

options.text: It waits for the other session, then puts 90 on top of the first 90
options.misconception: believes a version column queues two writes and adds them together

options.text: It stores 80, because the version column does the arithmetic itself
options.misconception: believes a version column performs the arithmetic the reader skipped

questions.explanation: The version column turns a silent clobber into a visible failure: the second write carries the version it read, that version is no longer current once the first write has moved it on, so the guarded statement matches no row and the run reported 0 rows changed. A caller that counts the rows it changed therefore knows the update failed and can read the balance again and retry, which is the whole purpose of the column. It does no arithmetic and it queues nothing, so the two writes never add themselves up to the correct 80 by themselves.
questions.hint: Ask how many rows the guarded statement managed to match.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a lost update escapes notice
questions.learningObjective: explain why neither session can see the fault in a lost update
questions.stem: Two readers of the same account row both see 100, each takes off 10, and each puts 90 back without checking anything in between. Explain why neither reader can tell that anything went wrong.

answer.exemplar: Each session read a value that was true at the moment it read, so neither was working from a mistake, and each then wrote a value that was correct given that reading, so neither wrote a mistake either. The fault only exists in the gap between the read and the write, where the two sessions overlapped and neither could see the other, and by the time the second write lands the first one is already gone from the record with no trace that it ever happened. The stored balance of 90 is a correct-looking number produced by a wrong history, which is why the two sessions both report success and the account is 10 short.

questions.explanation: A lost update is not an arithmetic error and not a bad read, so nothing in either session's own state is wrong and neither has anything to report. The two writes overlapped, each assuming it was alone, and the record keeps only the last of them, so the loss leaves no mark that either side can inspect. Under a lock held from the read to the write the two takings came out as 80, and under a version guard the second write matched no rows at all, so in both cases the problem is caught at the moment of the write rather than in the balance afterwards.
questions.hint: Ask each session what it read and what it wrote, and whether either was wrong.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a partial dependency creates an update anomaly
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism by which a partial dependency multiplies an edit
questions.stem: An enrolment table keyed on (student, course) stores the course's credits in every row where that course appears, and the course appears in two rows. Explain why this makes changing the credits harder than it looks.

answer.exemplar: The credits are not one fact written once but one fact written twice, in two rows that have no link to each other except the course value they share, so nothing in the table connects them or reminds anyone that both exist. Changing the credits means finding both rows, and a change made in only one of them leaves the table holding two different answers to a question about a single course, with nothing to say which is right. Moving the credits into a table keyed on the course makes the value single, so the edit is one row and the two answers cannot come to disagree, and the second normal form exists precisely to rule out this design.

questions.explanation: The cost is not the extra bytes but the extra place a fact has to be kept right, because duplication is invisible: nothing in the row says it is a copy, so a correct-looking edit that touches one of the two rows leaves the table self-contradictory rather than obviously wrong. The same shape produces an insertion problem, since a course with no students has no row in which to be recorded at all, and a deletion problem, since removing the last student of a course takes the course's credits with it. Splitting the facts into tables keyed on student and on course removes all three at once.
questions.hint: Ask what connects the two rows that both hold the credits.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why counting joined rows overstates a total
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism by which a non-unique join inflates an aggregate
questions.stem: A total is reported from line_items joined to categories on the category label, and it comes out at 16 where the line_items table on its own says 8. Explain the mechanism.

answer.exemplar: The join is not pairing rows, it is matching them, and the label it matches on is not unique on the categories side, so each of the three tool lines is not one row in the result but two, one for each category row carrying that label. Every quantity is therefore on the result twice, and any aggregate over those rows counts each real line once per match, which turns 8 into 16 and turns 3 lines into 6. The doubling happens before the aggregate ever runs, so no choice of function recovers the truth from those rows, and the only fixes are to match on the category's own identifier or to collapse the duplicates before totalling.

questions.explanation: A join builds one output row per pair of matching rows, so it multiplies whenever the joined column repeats on either side, and a label that reads the same in several category rows is exactly that case. Everything downstream sees the multiplied set: a count reports 6 where 3 lines exist and a sum reports 16 where the quantities are 2, 1 and 5. Reading the same figure from the line_items table without the join is the check that exposes it, and it costs nothing to run.
questions.hint: Ask how many output rows each line item produces, and why.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a blank and a zero are not interchangeable
questions.learningObjective: explain what collapses when a missing value is read as a recorded zero
questions.stem: A readings table holds a blank, a 0 and a 5, and a report treats the blank as a zero. Explain what that does to the figures the table produces.

answer.exemplar: A blank says a reading was never established, while a zero says a reading was taken and came back at zero, and the aggregates treat those very differently because a zero is a value and a blank is the absence of one. The sum happens to survive, at 5 either way, since the zero and the blank add the same nothing to a total, which is exactly what makes the confusion easy to miss. The count falls from 3 rows to 2 values, and the average falls from 2.5 to about 1.67, so a sensor that reported nothing is quietly reported as having read zero, and a report that cannot tell those apart is describing a machine that does not exist.

questions.explanation: The functions differ on purpose: a column count and an average both need to know how many values they are working from, and a blank refuses to be counted, whereas a zero insists on being included. Filling the blank with a zero before the query therefore changes the denominator and produces a lower average from the same three rows. The total is the one figure that survives, so checking only the total will not reveal the substitution, and the honest repair is to report the count of missing readings beside the average.
questions.hint: Ask which aggregates need to know how many values they are using.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The bargain an index makes
questions.learningObjective: explain what an index buys on reads and what it charges on writes
questions.stem: Adding an index to a table makes some queries much faster and every write a little slower. Explain the bargain, and what decides whether it is worth taking.

answer.exemplar: An index is a second, deliberately ordered copy of the key columns, so a read that can enter it finds the rows it wants by walking down to the right place instead of reading every row, and the gain grows with the table while the read stays flat. The cost falls on the other side of the ledger, because every inserted, updated or deleted row has to be filed in that ordered copy as well, and an update that changes an indexed column has to be removed from one place in the order and put in another. So the bargain is paid in write throughput and in storage, and whether it is worth taking depends on whether the table is read far more often than it is written.

questions.explanation: What decides it is the shape of the workload rather than the size of the table: a thousand rows inserted once and read for years pays for its index many times over, while a table rewritten as often as it is read pays the write cost for nothing. An index also only helps the queries that can enter it, so a column nobody filters or orders by is storage and write cost with no return, and a badly ordered pair of columns can be worse than useless by giving the impression of coverage. Reading the plan for each query is how you find out which of those cases you are in.
questions.hint: Ask how often the table is written against how often it is read.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a stored copy can fall behind
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism by which a denormalised copy diverges
questions.stem: Order lines store a copy of the product name so a report can read one table. The product is renamed, and the report now shows that product as two rows. Explain how that happens and what stops it.

answer.exemplar: The copy is a second value that the product table no longer knows about, and it is kept right only by someone remembering to update every place it was written, which is a rule held in a person's head rather than in the data. Once the rename happens, the lines written before it and the lines written after it disagree about the same product, and a report that groups on the copy cannot tell that disagreement from two genuinely different products, so the product splits into two rows without any error being raised anywhere. Keeping the copies in step in the write path stops it, and reading the product name through a join to its table avoids the second copy altogether at the price of the join the copy was added to avoid.

questions.explanation: A constraint declared on the product table can protect the product table and says nothing about the copies of its values lying around in other tables, which is why nothing objects when the rename happens and the copies simply go stale. The result is a report that is confidently wrong, since it names two products where there is one, and the error is invisible until somebody counts the products by hand. Either the write path updates the copies or the read path goes back to the source, and the choice is a trade between speed and a single version of the truth.
questions.hint: Ask what keeps the stored name in step, and who is responsible for that.
